newsitem.title: GERMANY: German IG Metall targets jobs in wage demand.
newsitem.headline: German IG Metall targets jobs in wage demand.

text.p: Germany's largest engineering union, the powerful IG Metall, on Tuesday laid out its pay demand for 1997, putting a clear emphasis on job security as a major goal of the pay negotiations.
The union's chairman Klaus Zwickel said after a meeting of IG Metall's management board that union leaders recommended a pay claim of between 4.5 and five percent for next year.

That headline range was immediately rejected by metal employers group Gesamtmetall, who said it would at most be willing to discuss a wage increase in line with inflation, currently at around 1.5 percent in Germany.
But IG Metall's Zwickel made it clear that as much as half of the overall wage claim could be effected through measures aimed at securing jobs rather than direct wage increases.

"We have been put under pressure by dramatic erroneous developments in employment policies," Zwickel told a news conference. "Job security will have the highest priority for IG Metall in the 1997 wage round."
The total wage demand of 4.5 to five percent is made up of two components, a 2.5 to three percent compensation for increased productivity and two percent for expected inflation.

"The productivity component of 2-1/2 to three percent, should be used exclusively for goals related to job security policies," Zwickel said, adding that the union's aim in terms of basic pay would be to secure real spending power.
Gesamtmetall chairman Werner Stumpfe in a statement appeared to accept the principle that real wages should not fall, but repeated earlier insistences that overall labour costs needed to be cut.
"Wage increases in line with inflation could be discussed -- but only if savings in contractual labour costs also follow," he said in the statement.
Economists however focused on Zwickel's emphasis on job security measures as potentially paving the way for a final agreement that might include a relatively modest wage increase.
"The industry is in the midst of structural changes that tend to dampen wage demands," said Timo Klein, senior German economist at analysis group MMS International.
Klein added that this could lead to a settlement involving a wage increase of between two and 2.5 percent.
Swiss bank UBS agreed in an investment note published after the wage demand announcement that the depressed state of the labour market was also likely to make for a lower final deal.
"We expect a much lower settlement in the forthcoming wage round, just above actual inflation," the bank said.

IG Metall some 18 months ago secured a pay deal for its members which was hailed as a huge victory for the unions, offering workers a 3.4 percent rise in May 1995 and a further 3.6 percent increase in November of that year.

But that high pay increase was seen as backfiring to some extent. Independent economists with hindsight blame that pay deal and others in the 1995 payround for helping to tip the German economy into a downturn late last year.
The 1997 pay claim comes at a time when the union is already at loggerheads with employers over a new law allowing firms to cut sick pay to 80 percent of the normal wage from 100 percent.
The union reached an uneasy truce with the employers' association on Monday after vast walk-outs last week made companies realise the union would not simply acquiesce to the reduction in benefits.
The employers agreed to urge companies to reverse decisions to implement the sick pay cut immediately in return for a pledge from the union to drop its protest campaign.

Zwickel, who will hold more talks with the employer side on the sick pay issue on Thursday, said it was unclear at the moment whether the dispute over benefit cuts would be merged into the 1997 pay negotiations.
